utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may respond to that, Mr. President, and I trust my colleagues across the well in the Prosecution's Office do this on a daily basis, because heaven knows I did it for 20 years on a daily basis, and that is when you look at pieces of evidence, confessions, a variety of other things, and you go through an area and you analyse this, as a professional, you come to certain positions, i.e., that this person has put forward a defence that is not credible but, in fact, is grounded in base motives for looting, burning, et cetera; and that they are criminals, and any excuse they give for other conduct is dispensed from -- is dispensed of by a Prosecutor when he or she comes to that conclusion. That is professionally what a Prosecutor does. And with regard to those particular issues, and there have been many, many issues raised by the Prosecution that they have put on the table, and here is a witness that has the capability, because of his experience to the area, to provide the Chamber with his conclusions as to what he saw, the information he had, and what he concluded, based on that information, and then what he did. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with the matter. I'm just -- of course, we are not talking about opinions in a rather general way, but we're talking about -- let's wait and see what happens, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will say, just to go back to the Prosecution's position, I would submit to Your Honour if we merely look at what the Prosecutor did with now General Lesley, then Colonel Lesley, they put together certain sequences of events and said, Based on these events, what can you tell us about the shelling and the pattern of this shelling? utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we go to the actual motion itself, going through A through N, there are, in fact, 14. I will concede that if we go to the cover sheet on the appendix, it mistakenly says "13." But there are, in fact, 14.

The text is now handed out to you by the usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Galovic. Please be seated. You will first be examined by Mr. Kehoe, and Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, can you state your name for the record and spell your last name?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Ivan Galovic, G-a-l-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, let me take you back to the 18th of May of 2009. Do you recall meeting members of the Gotovina Defence team that day, and did you sign a statement that day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could bring up 65 ter 1D2695, and if I could provide the witness with a hard copy which I've given to the usher. And I'm just waiting for it to come up on the screen in front of you as well. It looks like two English copies, I think. Mr. Galovic, do you recognise this statement that is before you that you signed on 18 May 2009?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: I do. That's the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review it before you came to court here today?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, in my discussions with you and some of my colleagues, you made some corrections to that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, with your permission, I'd just like to go through some of these corrections. And if we could turn to the second page of the statement, towards the bottom of the page in English, at the paragraph beginning: "At the pre-investigation stage ..." It should be the second -- that page for you, sir, at the bottom of the page, it now reads: "At the pre-investigation stage, the police may temporarily seize objects if there is a risk of deferral, and search apartments and persons under the conditions provided by law ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In our discussions, and correct me if I'm wrong, in our discussions you changed that sentence to read: "At the pre-investigation stage, if there was a risk of deferral, the police may temporarily seize objects," and you strike "if there is a risk of deferral," you strike those words, and continue on saying: "... and search apartments and persons under the conditions provided by law." And strike the rest of that from "and" to the latter part -- last part of that sentence with the words "by the law." Is that correct, sir? So you do --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that hearing you put it that way, there must have been a misunderstanding. I can't see it here on the screen. The corrections I made had solely to do with grammar. Nothing changed in substance, merely certain phrases were repeated, and it sounded a bit strange. So I only corrected it to the effect that if there is risk of deferral, police may temporarily seize items and conduct searches of the apartment -- the rooms and of the person. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me read it the way I believe you told us, and then you can tell me if it's wrong in that paragraph: "At the pre-investigation stage, if there is a risk of deferral, the police may temporarily seize objects and search apartments and persons under the conditions provided by the law."

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me take you to page 9 of the statement concerning the Gosici matter. And, Mr. President, at the beginning of the second line, there is just a typographical error. Where it says "were no members," that should be "were not members" coming from the Croatian to the English it should be "were not members." Going to the next sentence, where it says: "Ivica Petric and Nikola Rasic," in that sentence, instead of "Ivica Petric," it should be "Pero Perkovic"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the last page of your statement. Page 11 in the English -- the second-to-last page. Apologies. And I think it's the identical in the B/C/S, or I've been informed, where you note at the end of the answer concerning the number of prosecutions, you note that it says you prosecuted 744 persons for aggravated larceny and battery. You informed us that that was based on records that were in your office, but that some records of cases that you prosecuted were in other locations because of a change in territory; and that number should, in fact, be higher, and that the statistics that you provided to us were the accurate numbers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When I was giving the statement, I used the information at the disposal of the Public Prosecutors' Office of the Republic of Croatia. You will forgive me if I tell you that we did not deal that much with the statistics at that time. The data is correct insofar as it reflects the situation as it manifested itself at the time, and in the meantime the territorial jurisdiction changed so that whatever was under the jurisdiction of Knin, and this came under the jurisdiction of the Zadar County Public Prosecutor's Office, some of that jurisdiction went to Sibenik, more of it to the municipal structure in Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, and to a certain extent Karlovac and Gospic. Thus the disparity in the statistics. As for the records I refer to, that's something that was sent on a monthly basis to the Ministry of Justice and that specific data is correct and accurately reflects the figures of the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll get into those in one moment. But just going back to the statement, other than those clarifications that you gave us, does the statement that's before you, the statement that you gave to the Gotovina Defence team on the 18th of May, 2009, does that accurately reflect what you told to the Gotovina Defence team at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is the information contained in there true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: The information is true and accurate. However, as the jurisdiction changed, certain matters were, by way of necessity, lost. As a result, the situation cannot be presented as accurately as would be required, although I subsequently retrieved certain information which enabled me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What I'm talking about is the statement itself. Is the information that you provided in the statement that's before you, is that true and accurate to the best of your knowledge? Except for the changes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I examined you today on those same matters, in court today, would your answers be the same answers to the Trial Chamber that you gave to the Gotovina Defence team?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would move for the admission of 65 ter 1D2695.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1553.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kehoe, if we will at a later stage refer to pages, what pages in the English version will you refer to? Because the hard copy and the electronic version, we find no page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first correction that I brought to bear was on page 2, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first correction --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was towards the bottom of page 2, and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what page -- including cover page, where does it stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Including the cover page, it's page 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The cover page being page 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 1. Where it says witness statement being page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other change concerning Mr. Pero Perkovic is on page 9 of the English; and the correction concerning the statistics is on the top of page 11 in the English, all including the cover page as page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I advised the witness as to the purpose of the witness summary, and at this juncture we would ask permission to read that witness summary into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the witness summary for Witness Ivan Galovic. Mr. Galovic testified that he was appointed the district public prosecutor in Zadar on 28 December 1990 and has been in that position ever since. Almost throughout the war, the Zadar County State Attorney's Office was composed of the state attorney and two deputies. The witness testified regarding the role of the civilian police and military police in the prevention and discovery of perpetrators of criminal offences, the procedure for investigations under Croatian law, and the autonomous and independent nature of the State Attorney's Office. Prior to Operation Storm, the territorial jurisdiction of the Zadar County State Attorney's Office covered the areas of the territorial jurisdiction of the municipal courts in Zadar and Biograd na Moru. After Operation Storm, the territorial jurisdiction of the Zadar County State Attorney's Office expanded to cover the territories of the municipal courts in Zadar, Biograd na Moru, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, Donji Lapac, and Korenica. This latter territorial jurisdiction continued until 27 September 1997, when the law changed. The witness participated in processing the murders in the villages of Varivode and Gosici. The witness testified that there was never any pressure exerted on him to give up further prosecution. Based on the records that remained in his office after the law changed in 1995 -- 1997, excuse me, the witness testified that the County State Attorney's Office in Zadar prosecuted 13 perpetrators of murder very shortly after Operation Storm, involving a total number of 25 victims. The witness testified that the County State Attorney's Office in Zadar has no jurisdiction over the criminal offences of larceny, or aggravated larceny, only over robbery. The witness testified that nine persons were prosecuted for the criminal offence of robbery in his jurisdiction, and the Municipal State Attorney's Office in Zadar and Benkovac prosecuted 744 persons for aggravated larceny and larceny. However, the witness testified that the more accurate numbers of prosecutions are contained in his monthly reports from 1995 and 1996, which include case files that he did not have access to when he first compiled the numbers. These case files were later transferred from his office. The witness testified that it was very difficult to prosecute the criminal offences of arson and mining of houses because it was almost impossible to discover the perpetrators in such a large territory. The Municipal State Attorney's Office in Knin received 117 crime reports against unknown persons, and the Municipal State Attorney's Office in Zadar received a total of 166 crime reports. The witness testified that he believed that the motive of these cases was plunder and that the buildings were burned in order to conceal the crimes. That completes the summary, Mr. President. If I may proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, I would like to just touch on some of the items, and just brief clarification of some items in your written statement. We're not going to cover everything that's in there, because that's part of the record already; but I'd like to focus on some of your experiences working in the Government of Croatia since 1981. In page 2 of your statement, you indicate that you were appointed the district public prosecutor and have remained -- in Zadar on 28 December 1990 and have remained in that position ever since.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel speak a bit more slowly for the benefit of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. Galovic, can you explain the role of the district public prosecutor in the Croatian system? And if I can caution you the way they caution me, just take your time while you're doing that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Let me first correct you. I have been a public prosecutor for much longer. I started as an intern in the Municipal Public Prosecutor's Office in Zadar in early 1976. On the 28th of December, I was appointed county - or at the time it was called district public prosecutor - in the then District Public Prosecutor's Office in Zadar. Therefore, in my career as a public prosecutor, I have passed all the intermediate steps leading to the position I have right now. The post of the public prosecutor, under the Croatian legislation, is above all and primarily to deal with the prosecution of perpetrators of crimes. The detection of crime falls within the remit of the police, but the duty of the public prosecutor is to direct their job, with a view to bringing perpetrators of crimes to justice and have them tried. This was the role I performed at the time. It implied the filing of requests for the conduct of investigations, filing of -- or issuing indictments, launching investigations, and resorting to extraordinary legal remedies which we have under our legislation, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you -- Mr. Galovic, you just noted for us that the duty of the public prosecutor is to direct the police job with a view to bringing perpetrators of crimes to justice and have them tried, and that's at page 20, line 9. Can you just briefly explain the relationship between the public prosecutor, the police, and the investigative judge, in this entire prosecutive [sic] -- investigative process?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: The fundamental task of the police is to detect a crime and perpetrators thereof, as well as to gather evidence so that a criminal report could be filed with a public prosecutor. The public prosecutor, based on what is contained in the criminal report, decides on the course to be taken. One of the options is that if the criminal report does not contain sufficient elements for launching an investigation, then a request for additional processing has to be filed, or if there is enough information already, then an investigation is launched. It's the investigating judge who comes into play at this point, who decides on whether to launch the investigation. If the investigation is, indeed, launched, then this is the official start of the criminal proceedings. I'm highlighting this because it is only from this point onwards that we can speak of evidence in its own right. Whatever had been collected by the police before that point serves only as the initial material intended for launching proceedings and is, in fact, excluded from the file until such time as the investigation is closed. When the investigation is closed, the file goes back to the public prosecutor to decide if charges are to be brought or if prosecution is to be given up on. If it is decided that an indictment will be issued, then what ensues is a trial and then, of course, also the appeals proceedings, depending on the developments in the course of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, one point of clarity. You mentioned just now that there are -- is information that's collected by the police before the investigative judge comes in, and that serves as the initial material intended for launching the proceedings, but is not evidence, itself. Would that initial information that you're talking about, used to launch the proceedings, would those be the Official Notes that the police would put in the file?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, yes. Or, rather, for the most part it's the notes that constitute this sort of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last point of clarity. You noted that the investigation begins with the investigative judge after information is relayed to him, and he completes the investigation. Is there any type of criminal process in the Croatian system where you, as the public prosecutor or the municipal prosecutor, can issue a charging document without the investigating judge coming into the arena?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible. Let me only specify one issue: The investigation is launched on the basis of a request for the conduct of investigation, and the investigation will be closed only once the investigating judge has decided that everything that could be gathered or sufficient evidence has been gathered. And at that point the file goes back to the public prosecutor. I said that this case was possible where the public prosecutor disposes of good-quality material in the criminal report enabling him to proceed and directly issue an indictment. I think that this is valid for all the crimes which incur a maximum sentence of eight years, which could be the subject of direct indictments. During the war, because of the circumstances prevailing at the time, it was possible that the public prosecutor, in respect of each and every crime, regardless of the prescribed maximum sentence, could make such a direct decision to indict, depending, of course, on the material contained in the relevant criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And following up on that, Mr. Galovic: During this time-frame, did you, as the public prosecutor, yourself, or the colleagues that were working for you, did they file indictments or charges in the fashion that you just described?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such proceedings. I repeat, it always depended on the quality of material we had at our disposal. It boils down to the principle of economy or efficiency, if you have that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, let me direct your attention back to the period of time around Operation Storm. I'm talking about July, August, toward the end of 1995. Could you tell the Trial Chamber how many lawyers, attorneys, you had working with you in the District Public Prosecutor's Office in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: In my office, in the County Public Prosecutor's Office, there were two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how big was the rest of the staff, in addition to the two lawyers and yourself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me about Municipal Public Prosecutor's Offices, and I presume you do, one deputy was assigned to work in Knin. In the Municipal Public Prosecutor's Office in Zadar, together with the municipal public prosecutor, there were eight of them. There was the lady public prosecutor and seven deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In page 6 of your statement, you noted the jurisdiction -- the jurisdiction of the State Attorney's Office expanded after Operation Storm. After that expansion of the territory that you were covering, how many investigative judges did you have within this territory?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and remember. There was a military prosecutor in Zadar. I think there were other three, although I can't tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as you know, Operation Storm began on the 4th of August, 1995. Did you have any advance warning or knowledge that Operation Storm was going to take place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm a bit confused by the last answer. You were asked about how many investigative judges there were, and part of the answer was: "There was a military prosecutor in Zadar, I think there were other three." Are we talking about investigative judges, or are we military prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll ask him to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, my question to you was how many investigative judges did you have within your expanded territory after Operation Storm, and your answer was: "There was a military prosecutor in Zadar, and I think there were --"

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Not a prosecutor; an investigative judge, a military investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So that there was a military investigative judge and three other investigative judges? I'm getting some feedback here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me try this. Let me try this mike over here. I think that will work, Mr. President. We'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the three others that you were talking about, you were talking about three other investigative judges; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not certain, but, yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going back to my other question about Operation Storm, which took place on the 4th of August, 1995, did you have an advanced warning that Operation Storm was going to take place on the 4th of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no advanced warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After Operation Storm, did the work in your office increase?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: At least tenfold, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you say "tenfold," how long did this increase in work go on, where you say it was a tenfold increase?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the period in which the military courts functioned, until they were abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate date of that? Was it the end of 1995, into 1996; when was that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Late 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did you get any -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Let me add something. After that, all cases from the Military Prosecutor's Office were then transferred to mostly the municipal office, and some of them ended up in my office as well. This included all criminal offences against the Republic of Croatia. And to make it clear for you, I'll tell you this: In 1997, when those cases were deferred to us, since we kept records of persons, this included some 10.000 persons. Our ordinary yearly burden or workload would be 100 to 150 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, to meet this additional burden, Mr. Galovic, did you get additional resources?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. In the meantime, the number of deputies increased. I had one extra deputy. A year later, an additional two arrived, and the same team is at work even today. So five deputies in the crime -- Criminal Offences Department. I can tell you that all that enormous work is behind us now because all those cases fell under the application of the Law on Pardon. However, all those cases had to be checked to see whether they contained the elements of certain crimes which did not fall under that law. Only after having analysed the cases in such a way could we propose those cases to be included under the Law on Pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Taking the period after 19 -- after Operation Storm in 1995, with this increased workload you said was tenfold, I mean you said that -- I asked you whether or not your resources were increased, and you gave us some numbers. And my question to that is: Were these increases in resources adequate to meet this additional demand that was being placed on your office?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer that -- to that question. I'll tell you this: With additional effort, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit about that effort, and let's talk a little bit about the challenges. I mean, what else did you have to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could I ask some clarification of some of the answers. You said the workload was tenfold. You said a yearly burden was 100 to 150 persons, and you were talking about, in 1997, cases deferred to you, 10.000 persons. That seems to be 100 times rather than 10 times, or at least 70 to 100 times. So, therefore, I have difficulties in reconciling when you said it was tenfold, whereas it seems to be far more. Could you explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. It is difficult for me to say -- well, let me put it this way: The figures, themselves, do not adequately reflect the increase of workload. When I said "at least tenfold," what I meant was the difficulty in performing the task which, if I can say, we inherited from the Military Prosecutor's Office, in the terms of -- in terms of the cases which fell under the Law on Pardon. That's why I was trying to be cautious and not to deal with the figures which could be terrifying in themselves. But in my approximation, the additional burden was around ten times over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier used the word "deferred" to you in 1997. Do I take it from your last answer that they were deferred from the military prosecutor to your offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was in 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said this included offences against the state of Croatia. Are you referring to armed rebellion against the state of Croatia, these type of cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if you would skip those, so not talk anymore about these type of cases, could you tell us how the workload developed in relation to non-armed rebellion or linked cases? So that is thefts, murders, breaking and entering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The assessment that -- when I said that the increase was tenfold, it had to do with the municipal offices in Benkovac, Zadar, and Knin. Concerning the County Prosecutor's Office, the increase was mainly in terms of the crime of murder, because at that time we had 13 persons, 13 perpetrators, as well as 25 victims in the cases we processed. Before that, annually the rate of murders was five, at the most, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just by way of clarity on the questions Judge Orie was asking you, did this tenfold increase in work begin right after Operation Storm and go from there on into 1995 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Until the end of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to discussing the additional challenges that your office and the Municipal Prosecutor's Offices had with these increased demands. I mean, what did you do about that, and how did you try to meet these demands?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: There was a horrifying amount of work to be done. For example, in Knin, where I had one deputy, I told him expressly that he should proceed extremely resolutely and efficiently and to bring charges immediately based on what the material he received, since it was possible so as not to prolong any proceedings. Since there was a lot of work to be done, I organised it in such a way that, by way of necessity, he was helped by the personnel from the Zadar office because he was a deputy from Zadar. There was no other way to disseminate work. We, from the county office, helped as well. In any case, the meaning of it all was to deal with this increase promptly. We did our best in doing so, and I can tell you that I personally believe we succeeded to a great extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just to clarify this, we're talking about crime -- the tenfold increase after Storm, this tenfold increase, how much of it was related to crimes committed after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: All of them. All of the cases involved crimes committed after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned -- I'm sorry, did I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to say this: I don't know whether you're interested, but I can tell you what position I took concerning the crimes, what were my priorities. I can share that with you, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: My basic principle to make decisions at that time boiled down to promptly processing what could be processed. Specifically, that included the crimes of aggravated theft, theft, robbery, and this did not include murders because that required investigations. But concerning the crimes in which, for example, people were caught with stolen goods, such cases could and were promptly processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, staying with that, sir, I mean, why was that of such an interest to you? Why was this of such an interest to you, to promptly prosecute these theft and aggravated theft crimes with people who were caught with property? Did you have a greater goal in mind? If you can, explain it to us.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The situation was simply chaotic. It was necessary for the state, that is to say, for its judiciary, to send out a clear message that such things would not and could not be tolerated. That was what -- that was my driving force. If I tried to recollect that period, I often referred to it as the phenomenon of a stampede. Once the territory was liberated, those who had spent four years as refugees, and those people fell under one category, once they went into their villages they would come across their houses which had been completely looted, and most of them even destroyed or burnt down, they simply set out to get their stuff, as they often said. Their defence usually was that they were not stealing, but getting back what was theirs. Of course, we didn't tolerate that, except in those cases in which that could be proven. The other category, far more dangerous, comprised -- well, I don't know how this would be translated, but scavengers, those who always seized whatever moment or situation they could to loot and take away whatever they could, under any circumstances. I can tell you that they even looted my mother-in-law's weekend home in Karin, although I put a sign on the door saying "Ivan Galovic, county state prosecutor." It didn't help any. I found that sign somewhere in the garden later on, and everything was taken from the house. I don't even know how they managed to do so, given that the door was not a standard one; it is narrow. It all had to be dismantled, taken out. The only solution I saw in such a situation was to have such people processed promptly, so that all of those who did not follow in the same vein, by that point in time would be dissuaded from doing so and that the perpetrators be adequately processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were talking about this situation being chaotic, and you referred to your individual situation. And you mentioned that in the village of Karin, you had a sign up in front of the house. What did that sign say?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: It said "Occupied," and the name of a person; probably a JNA officer. And it also said "Mined." Later on, when I checked, I found out that it was not mined, but some houses in Karin were. I believe two looters lost their lives entering one of such houses, because to their misfortune, they entered a house that had been booby-trapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, I was talking about the situation in addition to the item that you just gave us - thank you - but the situation where you said that you had a sign with your name above your mother-in-law's house in Karin, and it was looted anyway?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that sign was taken off the door and thrown into the garden. I found it somewhere in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were houses around your mother-in-law's house or other buildings around your mother-in-law's house also looted, or was yours the only one?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: They were all looted, including the school building which was right next to my house, although there wasn't much to be taken away from there. Everything was being taken away; toilets, fridges, furniture, anything they could come across; that's why I called it a stampede.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to this looting, sir, were houses being burnt by these individuals as well?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: That was the most frequent modus operandi. Once they were done looting, they would set it on fire. In my belief, that was to cover up any traces. For the most part, it was for that reason. There may have been some other motives, but the primary motive was to loot, and then those houses, for the most part, would be set ablaze. When I talk about processing, it was relatively simple to prove that the crime of theft or looting occurred, but it was far more difficult to prove that the perpetrator in the case set the house on fire. A common defence at the time was that they were simply salvaging stuff from the houses which had already been on fire, no matter how ridiculous that sounded. They were saying that they were not looting, but simply saving the items from the houses which were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, let me just follow up on one of your answers that you gave. You said: "When I talk about processing, it was relatively simple to prove that the crime of theft or looting occurred, but it was far more difficult to prove that the perpetrator in the case set the house on fire." Can you elaborate on that for us and explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: I can refer you to the data. We had many reports for crimes against general security of people and property. That is the legal qualification. This included arson. We did not know and we could not detect the perpetrators. And in some 40 per cent of the cases, we couldn't even find the victims. We simply didn't know who owned those houses. For the qualification of the act itself, this was not relevant, but it was relevant in terms of the motive and any subsequent legal qualification and any eventual changes to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, in your work as the public prosecutor, was there a relationship between the prosecution of these individuals for theft and the prevention of arson?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you eliminate or take off the scene those who stole, then you would probably eliminate the cause of any further arson, if you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this looting that was taking place and, you know, the burning that was taking place, this Trial Chamber has heard a lot about check-points and police in the area, and police in the area that had the ability to stop this type of crime, to stop looting and burning in these areas. As the public prosecutor, what's your position on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that there were so many criminal reports submitted, which we then processed, speaks to the efficient conduct and work of the police in detecting the perpetrators. However, trying to apprehend all of them, given the size of the territory and given that a great many of those people were -- was domicile population who knew the terrain perfectly well, and they made good use of it, in my view it would have been possible to do more only if we had prevented anyone from entering that area. But you can't do that to a person who had been a refugee for four years and now wanted to go in to see what happened to his or her house. How can you prohibit that from happening? I believe the only way would have been, perhaps, to have a policeman escorting every single one of them to their home and again out of the territory. This is as graphic as I can get.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, on the looting issue, sir, you noted for us earlier in your testimony that one of the defences that suspects had presented was that they had their own -- what they were taking away was their own goods. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A great many of those people who were arrested at such check-points with stolen goods, for which there were reasonable grounds to believe they had been stolen, would say that that stuff was theirs or that they found them in some abandoned houses or in a neighbourhood, discarded. That was a rule, by way of the explanation they provided as to how they got to that stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in investigating their defence that the property they had was theirs, during your investigation did you ever find out that that was true?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: In several cases, yes. Or better put, we faced the problem of the principle in dubio pro reo. In cases in which we could not prove otherwise, we were forced to accept such defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, one last question, before we change topics, on the actual burning issue. Were you ever in Kistanje after Operation Storm, sir? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: I went through Kistanje on several occasions. The first time, it was when we were establishing the Court and the Prosecutor's Office in Knin. I was driving my deputy there to acquaint him with the nature and the amount of work that was before him. And then a few days -- a few times later, when I went to Knin to undertake supervisory -- supervision of his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, if Operation Storm commenced on the 4th, can you give us an approximate time of your first drive through Knin? Approximately, I'm not looking for an exact date. Sorry, not Knin, Kistanje. Your first drive through Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: It must have been between the 10th and the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Galovic, can you describe the level of burning that you observed in Kistanje during this time-frame when you drove through?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: At least to the extent of what one could see from the road while passing through the center of town, it did not appear dramatic, unlike Turanj, which is a place near Karlovac, which had the landscape as can be seen on the moon, where everything was torched and razed to the ground. Here, on the other hand, I did not observe anything that would go beyond what one would expect to find in the wake of such an operation. We did not receive a single report on that score in relation to Kistanje. At a later date, perhaps, yes, for Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm looking at the clock. I'm about to go into a series of reports with the witness at this juncture. I don't know if this is a propitious time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is, but I would like to seek one clarification. The last question that was put to you, you said you did not observe anything that would go beyond what one would expect to find in the wake of such an operation. Now, could you just give us a -- did you see houses that were burned? And if so, approximately the number that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I passed along the main road, I could see very few badly-damaged houses. It's been a long time ago, but what I can tell you about - how shall I put it? - with some degree of certainty is that the impression I gained in Kistanje was not to the effect that something out of the ordinary had happened there, or else I would have instructed the police to investigate into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That still does not answer my question. I asked you: Did you see any burned houses --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- burned to the extent that they could not be used anymore? So not a little bit of fire damage, but just burned houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you that there must have been several, but I can't be certain about it because, to go back to the answer which will not prove satisfactory to you, and I'm sorry about that, I did not have the impression that something had happened there which was not to be expected. There were damaged houses, but, in fact, my answer is I can't give you a precise answer. I can only speak in terms of my impressions. I can't tell you how many -- how many of such houses I saw, because I simply did not focus on the issue at the time. What I am sure of is that had it been to the degree that would have been memorable or etched in my memory, I would have noticed it, as I did, in fact, in Turanj and other such places where the extent of damage was that high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you well understood that this is not a real answer to my question. If you don't remember, fine, no problem. Did you see any house which was burned to an extent that it could not be used anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, I certainly did. But on hearing this question of yours, I'm trying to visualise what I saw at the time, and I'm unable to. It would be ridiculous to say that I didn't see anything of the sort. Unfortunately, I can't recall that scene in Kistanje which would leave the impression of total destruction, whereas I can do that in respect of some other places. I can't give you a better answer. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do I understand that you say, I saw at least one house which was burned to such an extent that it could not be used anymore, or do you say, I even don't remember that? Then I'd like to hear it so that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the former is true. In fact, I'm sure that the former is true, that I saw at least one house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you don't remember whether you saw a second house or a third house which also had been burned to an extent that it couldn't possibly be used anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I cannot give you a precise answer to. I can't give you an answer in quantitative terms. I can only speak about the impression I gained as I passed through Kistanje, and I can tell you what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The request to add 14 exhibits to the 65 ter list is granted. I do understand, Mr. Kehoe, that with some of these documents, you would like to deal with them in a rather exemplary way, just a couple of them, go through them, and then see whether it's necessary to go through all of them. That's an acceptable approach, and we'll see how it works out. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that score, Mr. Galovic, we would like to go and discuss for a bit some of your reports to the Ministry of Justice that you discussed previously, and I'd like to bring up 65 ter 1D2749 first. Now, Mr. Galovic, just taking a look at this report dated 19 October 1995 to the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Croatia, can you just tell us, initially, why was this report sent?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: In the briefest of terms, because the ministry sought it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I note that you have a series of these that we will talk about briefly that went to him on approximately a monthly basis. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in the paragraph that notes criminal offences against life and limb, it notes that: "Criminal charges have been filed against nine persons ..." And the reference is that the criminal offence is under Article 35(1) of the Code. And what is Article 34 -- excuse me, under Article 34 of the Code. What is Article 34?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 2, item 4, of that article, which is the qualified crime of murder, whereas one of the reports had to do with simple murder or ordinary murder, as it's called, under Article 34(1).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we move to the -- under section -- excuse me. Under the section that's noted for offences -- criminal offences against personal and moral degradation, and number 1 under that heading, we have criminal charges filed against two persons for the criminal offence described in Article 79(1) of the Code. What is Article 79?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: That's the crime of rape. I can see that proceedings were initiated against two individuals who were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn the page in the English, and I believe turning the page in the B/C/S as well, and looking under the heading "Criminal Offences Against Private and Public Property" at the top of the page. Now, before we turn to the actual number of 309, if I could just ask you, Article 127 of paragraph 2 of the Code, and Article 126, could you tell us what those two articles are, respectively?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: 127 is robbery; and 126, aggravated theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the number for that paragraph, it notes that criminal charges have been charged against 309 persons for criminal offences, for either robbery or aggravated theft. Of this number, are we talking about unknown perpetrators in this number of 309 or known perpetrators? Mr. President, I don't know if we're getting translation. Let me just ask again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to this number of 309, Mr. Galovic, are we talking about charges filed against unknown perpetrators or known perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: All of them were known. All the individuals were known, identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, of this 309 people, does this number include charges filed against individuals who are claiming the status or who at one time were in the HV?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, the answer is "no".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, can you, in this system -- so with regard to the individuals, this 309 people, there were people that were out of the HV, or what was their status of this 309 people, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: In these reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: These relate to civilians only. Had they -- or were they military personnel, then the report would have been filed with the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stay with that for one moment with regard to civilian status. And you had Home Guard units that were moving out of the area. Did you have some distinction between individuals who were HV soldiers or who were back at home, and what status they had, when you made a decision how to charge them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: It depended on the circumstances involved. The rule of thumb was that an individual, including military personnel, committed a crime, and if that person ceased being a member of the military, then the civilian court and not the military court had jurisdiction over it. It is possible, therefore, that certain individuals who committed crimes as military personnel, and were in the meantime demobilised, then they became -- or fell under the jurisdiction of a civilian court or a municipal court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, at page 41, line 7, the witness, I believe in Croatian, added something with respect to the time-frame as to when the person ceased being a member of the military, and if that could perhaps be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, we're not certain that we had the whole of your answer translated. You said: "The rule of thumb was that an individual, including military personnel, committed a crime, and a court, not the military court, had jurisdiction over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe you missed a line there, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry: " ... committed a crime, and if that person ceased being a member of the military, then the civilian court and not the military court had jurisdiction over it." Is part of your answer missing, especially in relation to when the person ceased being a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, it's the military court which has jurisdiction over military personnel. However, in the event where such a serviceman ceased being a member of the army before the indictment is issued, then it is the civilian court which has jurisdiction over that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That apparently clarifies the issue. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So going back to the -- just clarifying this, within this, for instance, 309 people who had charges filed against them, did that include a soldier who may have been arrested for looting while he was in the HV, demobilised, and then the charges were filed? Would it include a person like that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was not the case, although it is possible. And I can give you a negative answer to a pretty high degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you some further explanation on the difference between -- before we move on on this, on the difference between robbery and aggravated larceny. Could you give us what the legal distinction is between Article 126, aggravated larceny, and robbery in Article 127?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Simple theft or aggravated theft is a property crime, whereas robbery is a complex crime consisting of theft and force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Let us continue on with this report. And if we could move down to the next section, which notes the criminal offences against general safety of people and property, and it notes that two people -- charges were filed against two people for Article 155(1) in connection with Article 146(1). Could you explain that for us, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: That is the instance of setting houses on fire, and the two persons are the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, can you just explain, just briefly, the connection between Article 155 and 146, as it's set forth in there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Article 146 provides for the simple crime, and Article 155 is the qualified crime, crime qualified by the property-related damage. In other words, when talking about arson, it relates to the extent of damage. This is the briefest of explanation I can provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think if we go into the other criminal offences, and then the latter two pages we have a set of more -- any number of articles, Mr. President, they really are of very little consequence. The total, of course, at the bottom, you note that for this time-frame in the totals, criminal charges have been filed against 364 persons, and, in number 4, it is indictments were raised against 182 persons. Your Honour, at this time we'll offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2749.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you explained this to us briefly earlier today about, you know, theft crimes and arson crimes. And as we look at these reports, I mean, there are any number of theft crimes that you've charged, many of them with -- excuse me, if I can. There were 309 charged with theft crimes, and only two charged with arson charges. Is that an example of what you were talking about, the difficulties with charging arson, as opposed to theft crimes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. This transpires from the figures, themselves. It was relatively easy to prove theft, and it was almost impossible to detect most of the perpetrators of arson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move to the next document, which is 65 ter 1D2750. This is a report from the 23rd of November, 1995. Now, correct me, Mr. Galovic, if I'm reading this wrong. Is this -- and if we look at the general outset of this report from the 23rd of November, 1995, to the Ministry of Justice, under the criminal offences against private and public property, it notes that -- well, actually before then, the paragraph, it said: "With respect to the information delivered in our report of 19 October 1995, new information differs only in the following:" And under the crimes for -- against private and public property, you have filed against 705 persons. Now, these individual crimes, sir, these crimes against public property under Article 127 and 126, was this basically the largest -- was this basically the largest problem you had in the area, or the largest part of your caseload, dealing with these types of larcenist offences and robberies?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Not only was this the major problem, it also further complicated the situation by being the generator of all the subsequent crimes. The instances -- the high instances of theft engendered new crime. For instance, if an individual was caught in a house where theft was committed, unfortunately such a person -- if the person happened to be in a house where theft was committed, the person was quite often either injured or killed. In all the cases where this could be prevented, it was done so. I would be happy to tell you that the practice was more successful than it was, but unfortunately it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, tell me, sir, when you saw this increase in these types of theft and robbery crimes, was it -- were you presented with defences by the perpetrators, such as, Well, we were just conducting mop-up operations, or, We were out in the field in the end of August doing mop-up operations? Did you get that defence? And we're talking about -- I'm looking at these reports going into the latter part of 1995.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, there were frequent cases where such individuals tried to account for their conduct, which I called bestial in many instances, and I stand by that, by cushioning it into some sort of patriotism or duty, where in fact it constituted the worst possible type of criminality, and that's how I treated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you say that you treated it in that fashion, what, as the public prosecutor, did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: I brought charges in such a way that the contents of the indictment made it quite clear who the criminals were and of what type. In my mind, these were qualified murders for which the maximum sentence prescribed was that of 20 years of imprisonment. We didn't have any higher sentences under the legislation of the time. And I believe that to be an adequate response by the state to that sort of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we can move on to the last bit of the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, I would like to talk to you a little bit about this Varivode and Gosici investigation that begins in your report in 6 -- page 6 of -- not your report, your statement, D1553. And in your statement, you discuss the incidents of Varivode and Gosici. Just preliminarily, Mr. Galovic, can you explain to the Trial Chamber why these incidents were prosecuted in a civilian justice system and not a military justice system?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Because we treated those persons as civilians at the time of prosecution. This was never in dispute. This is an issue of subject-matter jurisdiction, and this is what the Court took care of. This was never in dispute, and I can explain to you why it was so, as well as why it was processed the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you do so, sir, could you explain it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: A group of persons was involved which, in a rather large area, although I'm not familiar with it in geographical terms, but I know which locations it includes, were robbing and killing civilians. Since Operation Storm had been completed quite some time before that, they could not have been in that area for any military tasks. They were doing this of their own accord, and this was proven by all the evidence involved. This was not in question. The crimes they committed were qualified as aggravated murders. Two of them were charged with 16 qualified murders each, so there was a total of 32 murders, seven plus nine, because there were two -- the two of them were both in Varivode and Gosici. Seven in Gosici; nine in Varivode; that's 16 for each of them. So 32 murders is what they were charged with, and then including -- as for the other indictees, they were charged with those murders that they participated in. I don't think we could have dealt with the issue in a more qualified or rigorous manner. I don't know whether you wish to ask me anything else. Perhaps you can ask me specific questions, and I can be as specific as you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This group that was committing these crimes, I mean, how large was this group of people? You talked to us previously about a group, and I refer you to page 49, line 15. It says: "A group of persons was involved which, in a rather large area, I'm not familiar with it in geographical terms ..." And I'm talking about the groups of persons. How large was this group that was committing these crimes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: As for the -- for the known perpetrators, there were seven or eight of them. There was indicia that there were several other persons included in the group, but up to that point in time we were unable to determine that. What we could ascertain is what we included in the indictment and processed, five of them for Gosici, four for Varivode, out of which two occur in the first group as well, so a total of seven accused; one who killed a person in Zrmanja, that's eight. I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we've been talking about murders for this group. Did your investigation reveal that these individuals were committing crimes other than murders?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: One couldn't talk of other crimes because the crimes, themselves, were qualified as aggravated murders, murders for gain, motivated by acquiring illegal gain. Specifically, this was simply taking away anything that they could get to; a calf, a sheep, a lamb, a car, a hunting rifle, depending on what it is that they found. They were simply roaming about the area for about a month, pillaging and committing a series of grave crimes. That was the result of our investigation, based on which we brought charges. The Court joined three of our indictments, that is to say, three proceedings which, in the investigation phase, were separate. They were subsequently joined in trial, which confirms that this involved a rather compact group. However, to my astonishment and very unpleasant surprise, the Court acquitted them of the most serious of crimes. Some of them were deemed guilty for individual murders, but as regards the most difficult and serious crimes in Gosici and Varivode, they were acquitted. After that, the County Prosecutor's Office in Zadar appealed the judgment and took it to the Supreme Court because of the erroneous factual basis. The Supreme Court accepted that appeal, and it quashed that part of the judgement, as well as repealing their appeal grounds in terms of the first-instance court decision, and they also rejected parts of our appeal which had to do with certain crimes encompassed by those indictments and concerning our appeal because of the sentence they received. We, as a matter of principle, appealed against the sentences pronounced in such crimes. Sometimes we were successful, but more frequently not so, unfortunately. What I need to state is that the decision of the Supreme Court was a confirmation that we did our work properly, that we qualified those crimes properly, and that there was a sound basis for our indictments. And in the new proceedings, I must confess, I expected that they would be sentenced. In the meantime, there was a change in territorial jurisdiction, and that case -- or those cases ended up in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the case is still outstanding, and if we could move into private session for one moment.

utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.text: Let me be more precise. utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's go -- continue on with the next one, which is yet another -- this is D145 [sic] that's MFI'd. It's another Official Note of Mr. Petric, dated 17 October -- excuse me, "1545," did I say that? D1545, MFI, yeah. Mr. Galovic, again looking at this particular document, as with the other one, is this another item that would have been in your file that you drew upon to decide whether or not to pursue this investigation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. By its very nature, it is the material contained in our file which is the supporting documentation to the criminal report. The police files the criminal report with a public prosecutor's office with all the supporting documentation which provided the basis for us, first, for investigations, then for the indictment, and ultimately for our appeal, in which we were successful. If we go through it and read it carefully, you will see that the gist of it is precisely what I was referring to, what sort of individuals these were and what they were doing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To -- I'm going to try to go through a series of documents right now, Mr. Galovic, all related in the same time-frame, and just showing you each one, as opposed to doing them one at a time, if I can. utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can turn to the next one, which is -- I'm sorry. It is 65 ter 1D2730, and this is yet another Official Note by Mr. Rasic, by the police, where Mr. Rasic talks about the murders in Zrmanja. Mr. President, if I could have an MFI number for this at this juncture. If we can just MFI them. We do them as a group, Mr. President, so 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's one which is not yet in the series.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just take a moment to address this Court? We have received two information sheets, supplementary information sheets, as to what information this witness has provided in the course of the proofing sessions, and none of these notes, in fact, indicate that this witness was shown these documents and what he has, in fact, said about those documents in the course of the proofing sessions. And I believe the proofing session -- the notes are to give us notice as to what, in fact, has -- what information the witness has provided in relation to documents shown to him, so perhaps -- but Mr. Kehoe can tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, number 1, it's in his statement concerning this entire matter. Number 2, I gave notice to the Prosecution that we were going to use these documents in discussions with Mr. Galovic. If I may, we have a series of documents on page 8 of the statement. But, you know, in any event, Mr. President, this is the subject of discussion that goes on, on numerous pages in the statement concerning the -- Gosici and Varivode. And if we look at the pages, themselves, we start on page 6, 7, going back over into 8, where those are all issues that are referred to in some length by the witness. So I don't know what else the Prosecution wants by way of a supplemental information sheet. Certainly, these documents weren't a surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that wasn't my point. My point was Mr. Kehoe's question indicated that the notes had been shown to the witness either yesterday or today. That's, as I recall, what I gathered. And, in fact, the statement has been compiled much before, not yesterday or today. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record now. Any consequence, in your view, to be attached to what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE

utterances.text: It's on the record. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Kehoe. How much time would you still need? Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I simply have, Mr. President, these particular -- the rest of these exhibits just to show the witness and say, Take through the sequence and say was this part -- I was just going to show them one by one and then just ask an overall question concerning these Official Notes being part of the file when you were making a decision to pursue an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, would there be -- are these some of the series we have already, or are these new ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These are all the same series, Mr. President. The last one is the only one that had not been in the series to date.

utterances.text: Yes. utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's try to resolve it in a practical way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. -- just going through the rest of these, Mr. Galovic, have you seen Official Notes by Mr. Nikola Rasic, Zlatko Ladovic, Zeljko Mijic, Milenko Hrstic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Hrstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right. That's the only Croatian name I can't get right. That was a private joke. Hrstic. Those are -- all of those, sir, have you seen those and reviewed those, and were they part of your file, and did you take those into consideration to determine whether or not you were going to pursue an investigation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. They were part of my file. All of them were part of the file on the basis of which we took our decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last question, sir. And you mentioned some of this in your statement. But specifically, has anyone ever told you not to prosecute a crime, when you were acting as the public prosecutor? Has anybody told you or ordered you not to prosecute someone for a crime?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC
utterances.text: Never. To me, never. I don't really know -- I can't even picture what that sort of situation would be, where somebody would ask me to do that, and I can tell you that nobody ever dared tell me to take decisions that would in any way go out of what was prescribed by the law. And I can tell you that all the decisions I made, I made them independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Galovic. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. I'd like to put on the record that the Chamber received an internal memorandum sent by Mr. Monkhouse, copied to the parties, in which he deals with the decision of this Chamber to assign numbers to the series of documents. And there were these other reports sent by the witness to the Ministry of Justice. There were no objections, Ms. Mahindaratne?
